summary:
Misiones province stands under Argentina's national framework. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012; it permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. The national identity document has carried an "X" marker since 2021, marriage equality has been available since 2010, and anti-discrimination protection rests on a combination of national and provincial laws.

The statute has not been repealed, but executive action has narrowed its practical reach. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree restricting adolescents' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, reported as DNU 62/2025, alongside a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached its worst level in the ten years monitored by Argentina's national hate-crime observatory. At least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity were recorded during 2025, a 62% increase on the previous year and an average of one every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 142 of the 227 victims, or 62.5%. In 147 cases, 64.8%, the harm was physical violence against bodily integrity, with beatings the main modality. Perpetrators were predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space.

Trans activists interviewed in the national capital on 4 April 2025 by the Washington Blade said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate. They reported that the 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice.

On 5 April 2025 the Supreme Court of Argentina left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina was the first country in Latin America to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and it entered the period covered here with a regional reputation for pioneering transgender rights. Against that background an Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration rather than a break in the statutory text.

The national hate-crime observatory attributes the 2025 surge to the government's "cultural battle" and to hate discourse from official sources, a causal reading published alongside the figures rather than an independent finding. Agencia Presentes reported the counts on 19 March 2026 and described the year as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

Trans organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins were among those speaking to the Washington Blade on 4 April 2025, which situates the current atmosphere alongside a longer record of targeted killings of visible trans figures.
localsOnly:
The federal Trans Labor Quota Law reserves 1% of public-sector posts for trans workers. Activists told the Washington Blade that the Milei government dismissed trans hires made under the quota and that the law is no longer being implemented, a claim about administrative practice rather than about the statute's text.

The national Ministry of Women, Gender and Diversity was eliminated by the Milei government, removing the cabinet-level body that had carried policy for the community. Argentina's anti-discrimination protection continues to rest on a combination of national and provincial laws, so residents of Misiones are covered by both layers.

The second 2025 decree governs where transgender people are held in prison, a resident-facing rule that affects detainees rather than visitors. Provincial anti-discrimination and public-employment rules in Misiones were not covered by any source in this inventory.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory concerns Misiones specifically. There is no reporting here on provincial police conduct, provincial courts, documentation practice at the Misiones registry, local facilities, or hospital and school implementation of the 2025 decree on minors; the province appears only as a unit of the national framework.

The outcome of the litigation filed against the decree restricting gender-affirming care for minors is unresolved in the sources available here. Whether the decree is applied in Misiones public facilities is not sourced.

The hate-crime counts are national, with no provincial breakdown, so the 227 cases cannot be apportioned to Misiones. The claim that the 2012 law is "no longer guaranteed" is the assessment of the activists interviewed and is not a legal finding; the statute remains formally in force.

Implementation of the 1% public-sector trans quota within the Misiones provincial administration is not sourced either way.
